history.q: From which country did Kenya gain independence in December 1963?
history.fact: Independence came on 12 December 1963, now celebrated every year as Jamhuri Day.

history.q: Who led Kenya to independence and became its first president?
history.fact: Kenyatta was prime minister at independence and served as president from 1964 until his death in 1978.

history.q: What name is given to the 1950s armed uprising against British colonial rule in Kenya?
history.fact: Its fighters called their movement the Kenya Land and Freedom Army; Britain declared a state of emergency in 1952.

history.q: Which Portuguese explorer stopped at Malindi in 1498 and found a pilot to guide him to India?
history.fact: A stone pillar he erected on the shore at Malindi still stands today.

history.q: Which European power built Fort Jesus in Mombasa in the 1590s?
history.fact: The fort was designed by Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: What nickname was given to the nearly complete 1.5-million-year-old skeleton found near Lake Turkana in 1984?
history.fact: Spotted by fossil hunter Kamoya Kimeu, he is one of the most complete early human skeletons ever found.

history.q: Which family of fossil hunters made many celebrated discoveries of early humans in Kenya?
history.fact: Louis, Mary, their son Richard, Richard's wife Meave and daughter Louise all worked on human origins.

history.q: Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu grew rich as city-states of which Indian Ocean coastal culture?
history.fact: The Swahili language blends a Bantu grammar with many Arabic, Persian and later Portuguese and English words.

history.q: Nairobi was founded in 1899 as a depot on which railway?
history.fact: Its name comes from the Maasai phrase 'Enkare Nyrobi', meaning 'cool water'.

history.q: In 1898, two man-eating lions killed railway workers at which Kenyan river crossing?
history.fact: Engineer John Henry Patterson shot the lions; their skins and skulls are now displayed at the Field Museum in Chicago.

history.q: Kenya became a republic in which year, one year after independence?
history.fact: On 12 December 1964 the British monarch ceased to be head of state, and Jomo Kenyatta became president.

history.q: Until 1963, the narrow coastal strip of Kenya officially belonged to which ruler, though Britain administered it?
history.fact: The ten-mile-wide strip, including Mombasa, was transferred to Kenya at independence.

history.q: Which Mau Mau leader, captured in 1956, is honoured by a statue in central Nairobi?
history.fact: His bronze statue, unveiled in 2007, shows him holding a rifle on the street that bears his name.

history.q: Kenya's independence constitution was negotiated at conferences held in which London building?
history.fact: Conferences there in 1960, 1962 and 1963 paved the way for majority rule and independence.

history.q: Which chartered company administered British interests in Kenya from 1888 before the protectorate was declared?
history.fact: The company struggled financially, and Britain took direct control as the East Africa Protectorate in 1895.

history.q: When the East Africa Protectorate became a colony in 1920, what was it named after?
history.fact: Mount Kenya, at 5,199 metres, is Africa's second-highest mountain.

history.q: The 'airlift' that sent hundreds of Kenyan students to US universities from 1959 was organised chiefly by which politician?
history.fact: Future Nobel Peace laureate Wangari Maathai was among the students who went to study in the US.

history.q: Which city was the capital of the British East Africa Protectorate before Nairobi?
history.fact: As the colony's main port and the starting point of the railway, Mombasa was the natural first seat of government.

history.q: Jomo Kenyatta and five other nationalist leaders were tried in 1952-53 in which remote town?
history.fact: The 'Kapenguria Six' were convicted and imprisoned; the trial is now widely seen as politically motivated.

history.q: Thimlich Ohinga, a UNESCO site near Lake Victoria, is famous for what?
choices: Dry-stone walled enclosures built without mortar
history.fact: The enclosures, probably first built in the 16th century, sheltered communities and their livestock.

history.q: Which power captured Fort Jesus in 1698 after a siege lasting nearly three years?
history.fact: The fall of Fort Jesus ended Portuguese dominance on the coast north of Mozambique.

history.q: In the early 1400s, envoys from Malindi presented a giraffe to the court of which empire?
history.fact: Courtiers hailed the giraffe as a qilin, a mythical creature whose appearance was a sign of good fortune.

history.q: The ruins of Gedi, a Swahili town abandoned in the 1600s, lie near which coastal town?
history.fact: Gedi's coral-stone palace, mosques and houses are hidden in a coastal forest close to Watamu.

history.q: Critics nicknamed the costly Uganda Railway what?
history.fact: Built from 1896 to 1901 largely by labourers from British India, it ran from Mombasa to Lake Victoria.

history.q: Which Kenyan paleoanthropologist became head of Kenya's wildlife service in 1989, the year a huge stockpile of seized ivory was publicly burned?
history.fact: The televised ivory burn helped build global support for the international ban on the ivory trade.

technology.q: Which pioneering mobile money service was launched in Kenya in 2007?
technology.fact: Launched by Safaricom, it let people send money by text message, even from basic phones without internet access.

technology.q: In Swahili, what does the 'Pesa' in M-Pesa mean?
technology.fact: The 'M' stands for mobile, so the name simply means 'mobile money'.

technology.q: Kenya generates much of its electricity from which renewable source tapped beneath the Rift Valley?
technology.fact: Kenya is Africa's leading producer of geothermal power, drawing on volcanic heat beneath the Great Rift Valley.

technology.q: The Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway, opened in 2017, was financed and built with help from which country?
technology.fact: It was the largest infrastructure project in Kenya since independence.

technology.q: Nairobi's thriving technology and start-up scene is often nicknamed what?
technology.fact: International tech firms have opened African offices in Nairobi, drawn by its strong mobile and start-up culture.

technology.q: Kenya is one of the world's leading exporters of which crop?
technology.fact: Kenya is the world's largest exporter of black tea, much of it sold at the Mombasa tea auction.

technology.q: Which Kenyan city is East Africa's busiest seaport?
technology.fact: Mombasa's Kilindini Harbour also handles much of the trade of landlocked Uganda, Rwanda and South Sudan.

technology.q: Nairobi's main international airport is named after whom?
technology.fact: Jomo Kenyatta International Airport is the main hub of Kenya Airways and one of Africa's busiest airports.

technology.q: Kenya's fossil-rich Lake Turkana basin is especially important for the study of what?
technology.fact: Its sediments have yielded fossils of several early human species spanning millions of years.

technology.q: What is the name of the passenger train service on Kenya's Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway?
technology.fact: Madaraka means 'self-rule'; the service launched on 31 May 2017, on the eve of Madaraka Day.

technology.q: When inaugurated in 2019, the Lake Turkana Wind Power project was Africa's largest what?
technology.fact: Its 365 turbines take advantage of strong, steady winds funnelled between two mountain ranges.

technology.q: Many of Kenya's export flower farms are clustered around which Rift Valley lake?
technology.fact: Roses cut in Kenya in the morning can be on sale in European cities within days.

technology.q: Which country operates the Broglio Space Centre off Kenya's coast near Malindi?
technology.fact: Its sea platforms near the equator gave rockets an extra boost from Earth's rotation.

technology.q: Ushahidi, the Kenyan crowdsourced mapping platform created in 2008, takes its name from a Swahili word meaning what?
technology.fact: It was created to map citizen reports of violence after the 2007 election and has since been used in disasters worldwide.

technology.q: M-Kopa, founded in Kenya in 2011, became known for selling what on a pay-as-you-go basis?
technology.fact: Customers pay small daily instalments via mobile money; 'kopa' means 'to borrow' in Swahili.

technology.q: Kenya's Olkaria geothermal power plants lie in and around which national park?
technology.fact: Steam vents and towering cliffs give the park its name; visitors can cycle among zebras and giraffes.

technology.q: Which slogan is used by Kenya's national carrier, Kenya Airways?
technology.fact: Kenya Airways was founded in 1977 after the collapse of the shared East African Airways.

technology.q: Which Kenyan town is the centre of the country's main tea-growing region?
technology.fact: Rolling tea estates surround the town, whose high altitude and regular rainfall are ideal for tea.

technology.q: NASA's first X-ray astronomy satellite, launched from off Kenya's coast in 1970, was given what Swahili name?
technology.fact: Uhuru, meaning 'freedom', was launched on 12 December 1970, the seventh anniversary of Kenya's independence.

technology.q: What did researchers announce finding at Lomekwi, near Lake Turkana, in 2015?
technology.fact: The tools are about 3.3 million years old, older than the earliest known members of the genus Homo.

technology.q: SL28 and SL34, prized Kenyan coffee varieties, were developed in the 1930s by which institution?
technology.fact: SL28 was selected for drought resistance and is now celebrated by roasters for its intense, fruity flavour.

technology.q: Kenyan entomologist Thomas Odhiambo founded which Nairobi research centre in 1970?
choices: International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology
technology.fact: ICIPE studies insects to fight crop pests and diseases such as malaria in environmentally friendly ways.

technology.q: Kenya's Lake Magadi has long been mined for which mineral?
technology.fact: The shallow alkaline lake's trona crust is used to make soda ash for glass and detergents.

technology.q: Kenya's first satellite, the cubesat 1KUNS-PF, was built by which institution and deployed in 2018?
technology.fact: The tiny satellite was deployed into orbit from the International Space Station.

technology.q: What is Konza Technopolis?
choices: A mobile phone factory in Mombasa
A planned smart city and tech hub south-east of Nairobi
technology.fact: Billed as Kenya's future 'Silicon Savannah' city, it is being developed along the Nairobi–Mombasa highway.

art.q: Which Danish author wrote 'Out of Africa' about her years on a coffee farm near Nairobi?
art.fact: The 1985 film adaptation starring Meryl Streep and Robert Redford won seven Oscars, including Best Picture.

art.q: Which Kenyan author wrote the novels 'Weep Not, Child' and 'Petals of Blood'?
art.fact: 'Weep Not, Child' (1964) is often described as the first English-language novel published by an East African author.

art.q: The phrase 'Hakuna Matata', made famous by Disney's 'The Lion King', comes from which language?
art.fact: It means 'no worries' and was a popular phrase on the Kenyan coast long before the 1994 film.

art.q: Which Kenyan community is famous for colourful beadwork and the 'adumu' jumping dance?
art.fact: In the adumu, young warriors take turns leaping straight up from a standing position, as high as they can.

art.q: Which actress, raised in Kenya, won an Academy Award for her role in '12 Years a Slave'?
art.fact: She won Best Supporting Actress in 2014, becoming the first Kenyan to win an Oscar.

art.q: Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is famous for intricately carved what?
art.fact: Lamu is considered the oldest and best-preserved Swahili town in East Africa, with no cars in its narrow streets.

art.q: Which Kenyan Afro-pop band, formed in Nairobi in 2005, is known for hits such as 'Suzanna' and 'Sura Yako'?
art.fact: The group sings in a mix of Swahili and English, blending Afro-pop, soul and Kenyan benga.

art.q: Which Nairobi landmark has a cylindrical tower and a cone-shaped hall inspired by a traditional hut?
art.fact: Completed in 1973, the KICC was designed by Norwegian architect Karl Henrik Nøstvik and has a helipad on its roof.

art.q: The town of Kisii in western Kenya is famous for carvings made from what material?
art.fact: The soft stone is quarried at nearby Tabaka and carved into bowls, animals and abstract figures.

art.q: A kanga, the colourful printed cloth worn on Kenya's coast, traditionally carries what along its border?
art.fact: Women sometimes choose a kanga for its message, using the saying to communicate indirectly with others.

art.q: Benga, a Kenyan popular music style that emerged in the 1960s, is driven mainly by which instrument?
art.fact: Its fast, finger-picked guitar lines echo traditional string instruments; D.O. Misiani was hailed as one of its kings.

art.q: Which 2005 film based on a John le Carré novel was shot partly in Nairobi's Kibera and near Lake Turkana?
art.fact: Rachel Weisz won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role in the film.

art.q: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's 1986 essay collection arguing for writing in African languages is called what?
art.fact: After it, Ngũgĩ wrote his fiction mainly in Gikuyu, often translating it into English himself.

art.q: Which sung-poetry music genre, with Arabic and Indian influences, is popular on Kenya's Swahili coast?
art.fact: Taarab orchestras may combine the oud, violins and qanun with Swahili lyrics full of wordplay.

art.q: What is a kiondo, a well-known Kenyan handicraft?
art.fact: Kiondos are woven by hand from sisal fibres, often with leather straps and brightly dyed patterns.

art.q: Which Nairobi street-music genre, sung largely in Sheng slang, exploded in popularity in the late 2010s?
art.fact: Sheng mixes Swahili, English and other Kenyan languages and is the everyday slang of Nairobi's youth.

art.q: Which Kenyan band recorded the 1982 tourist-favourite hit 'Jambo Bwana'?
art.fact: The song's chorus of 'Hakuna matata' became a staple at hotels along the Kenyan coast.

art.q: The melody of Kenya's national anthem, 'Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu', is based on what?
art.fact: A commission adapted the tune from a lullaby of the Pokomo people for Kenya's independence in 1963.

art.q: Wanuri Kahiu's 'Rafiki' (2018) was the first Kenyan feature film selected for which festival?
art.fact: The film premiered in the festival's Un Certain Regard section.

art.q: Which Kenyan writer's satirical essay 'How to Write About Africa' became one of Granta magazine's most-shared pieces?
art.fact: Wainaina, who won the Caine Prize in 2002, also founded the literary magazine Kwani?

art.q: Which novel by Margaret Ogola follows four generations of Kenyan women?
art.fact: The 1994 novel won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize for best first book in the Africa region.

art.q: The 'Utendi wa Tambuka', one of the oldest known Swahili manuscripts, is what kind of work?
art.fact: Composed in the 1720s on the island of Pate, it tells of a battle fought by the early Muslim community.

art.q: In 2019, Kenyan-born artist Wangechi Mutu's bronze figures filled the facade niches of which museum?
art.fact: Her four seated women, 'The NewOnes, will free Us', were the first sculptures commissioned for the Met's facade.

art.q: Isukuti, a fast drum-led dance from western Kenya, was added to which UNESCO list in 2014?
choices: Intangible heritage in need of urgent safeguarding
art.fact: Isukuti is named after its long drums and is performed at births, weddings, funerals and festivals.

art.q: Which 2012 film became Kenya's first official submission for the foreign-language Oscar?
art.fact: Directed by Tosh Gitonga, it follows a young aspiring actor who moves from the countryside to Nairobi.

politics.q: Who served as Kenya's second president, from 1978 to 2002?
politics.fact: A former teacher, Moi was nicknamed 'Nyayo', Swahili for 'footsteps', after his pledge to follow in Kenyatta's.

politics.q: Which Kenyan president was the son of the country's first president?
politics.fact: Uhuru, whose name means 'freedom' in Swahili, served as president from 2013 to 2022.

politics.q: In 2004, which Kenyan environmentalist became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize?
politics.fact: Her Green Belt Movement, founded in 1977, mobilised women to plant tens of millions of trees.

politics.q: Under Kenya's 2010 constitution, parliament consists of the National Assembly and which other house?
politics.fact: Each of Kenya's counties elects one senator, and the Senate protects the interests of the counties.

politics.q: What is Kenya's national motto, meaning 'let us all pull together'?
politics.fact: Harambee also names a tradition of community fundraising, used to build schools, clinics and water projects.

politics.q: Which animals hold the shield on Kenya's coat of arms?
politics.fact: The lions stand on a green mountain representing Mount Kenya, decorated with crops such as coffee, tea and maize.

politics.q: What kind of government does Kenya have under its 2010 constitution?
politics.fact: The president is both head of state and head of government and may serve at most two five-year terms.

politics.q: Which United Nations agency has its global headquarters in Nairobi?
politics.fact: Nairobi is home to one of the UN's four major headquarters and the only one in the Global South.

politics.q: Who succeeded Daniel arap Moi as Kenya's president in 2002?
politics.fact: An economist trained at the London School of Economics, Kibaki served two terms until 2013.

politics.q: Into how many counties is Kenya divided under its 2010 constitution?
politics.fact: The counties, each with an elected governor and assembly, replaced Kenya's eight provinces after the 2013 elections.

politics.q: In which year did Kenyans approve their current constitution in a referendum?
politics.fact: The constitution was promulgated on 27 August 2010 in a ceremony at Uhuru Park in Nairobi.

politics.q: Which party governed Kenya continuously from independence until 2002?
politics.fact: The Kenya African National Union was founded in 1960; Kenya was legally a one-party state from 1982 to 1991.

politics.q: In which year did Kenya restore multi-party politics by repealing the one-party clause of its constitution?
politics.fact: The first multi-party general election in decades followed in December 1992.

politics.q: Who was Kenya's first vice-president, appointed in 1964?
politics.fact: He resigned in 1966 and went on to found an opposition party, the Kenya People's Union.

politics.q: Who served as Kenya's prime minister from 2008 to 2013?
politics.fact: The post was created by a 2008 power-sharing agreement and abolished under the 2010 constitution.

politics.q: Who was Kenya's first deputy president under the 2010 constitution?
politics.fact: The office of deputy president replaced the vice-presidency and was first filled after the 2013 election.

politics.q: Kenya is a founding member of which regional bloc, headquartered in Arusha, Tanzania?
politics.fact: First founded in 1967, the bloc collapsed in 1977 and was revived in 2000 by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

politics.q: What does the shield at the centre of Kenya's flag represent?
politics.fact: Black stands for the people, red for the blood shed for independence, green for the land and white for peace.

politics.q: In 2017, Kenya's Supreme Court became the first in Africa to do what?
politics.fact: The September 2017 ruling ordered a fresh presidential election, held the following month.

politics.q: What was the title of Jomo Kenyatta's 1938 anthropological study of his own people?
politics.fact: Kenyatta wrote it after studying anthropology at the London School of Economics under Bronisław Malinowski.

politics.q: What was the name of the system of regional governments in Kenya's independence constitution?
politics.fact: The regional assemblies were soon weakened and abolished as power was centralised in the 1960s.

politics.q: Who became the first African appointed to Kenya's colonial Legislative Council, in 1944?
politics.fact: Mathu, an Oxford-educated teacher, was nominated to the council by the colonial governor.

politics.q: Who became the first woman elected to Kenya's parliament, in 1969?
politics.fact: She had already made history in 1965 as Kisumu's mayor, the first woman to lead a Kenyan town.

politics.q: Who became Kenya's first chief justice under the 2010 constitution, taking office in 2011?
politics.fact: Mutunga was chosen through public interviews, a first for the office.

politics.q: Which Kenyan independence leader and trade unionist was assassinated in Nairobi in July 1969?
politics.fact: Mboya was only 38 years old; a major street in central Nairobi, Tom Mboya Street, now bears his name.

current-affairs.q: In October 2019, Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon distance in under two hours, in which city?
current-affairs.fact: He ran 1:59:40 with rotating pacers and a pace car, so the run was not eligible as an official world record.

current-affairs.q: Who won Kenya's presidential election held in August 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Ruto was sworn in on 13 September 2022 as Kenya's fifth president.

current-affairs.q: In October 2023, Kelvin Kiptum set a men's marathon world record in which city?
current-affairs.fact: He ran 2:00:35 in only his third marathon. Kiptum died in a road accident in February 2024, aged 24.

current-affairs.q: At the Paris 2024 Olympics, Faith Kipyegon won her third straight Olympic title in which event?
current-affairs.fact: She had also won the 1,500 m at Rio 2016 and at Tokyo 2020, becoming the first woman to win the event three times.

current-affairs.q: Which city hosted the first Africa Climate Summit in September 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Leaders adopted the Nairobi Declaration, calling for more climate finance and a global carbon tax regime.

current-affairs.q: On 13 November 2023, Kenya held a special public holiday dedicated to which activity?
current-affairs.fact: Citizens were urged to plant 100 million seedlings in a single day as part of a national greening drive.

current-affairs.q: In early 2020, Kenya suffered its worst outbreak in 70 years of which pest?
current-affairs.fact: Some swarms were reported to cover areas larger than a big city, devouring crops and pasture.

current-affairs.q: In September 2023, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania were chosen to co-host which tournament in 2027?
current-affairs.fact: The joint 'Pamoja' bid made it the first edition of the tournament to be shared by three host nations.

current-affairs.q: Which celebrated Kenyan novelist died in May 2025, aged 87?
current-affairs.fact: Author of 'Weep Not, Child' and 'Petals of Blood', he was long tipped as a contender for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

current-affairs.q: The Tokyo 2020 Olympic marathons, held in August 2021, were moved to which cooler Japanese city?
current-affairs.fact: Kenya won both: Eliud Kipchoge retained his title and Peres Jepchirchir took the women's race.

current-affairs.q: Kenya's first operational Earth-observation satellite, Taifa-1, was launched in April 2023 on whose rocket?
current-affairs.fact: The satellite was built by Kenyan engineers with a Bulgarian partner to monitor farming and the environment.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, Martha Koome became the first woman to hold which Kenyan office?
current-affairs.fact: As Chief Justice she also presides over Kenya's Supreme Court.

current-affairs.q: In June 2024, Kenyan police officers arrived to lead a UN-backed multinational security support mission in which country?
current-affairs.fact: The mission was authorised by the UN Security Council in October 2023 to help Haiti's national police.

current-affairs.q: From January 2024, what did Kenya introduce in place of visas for most visitors?
choices: A tourist tax paid on arrival
current-affairs.fact: Travellers apply online before their trip; the change was promoted as making Kenya open to visitors from everywhere.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, which legendary motorsport event returned to the World Rally Championship after a 19-year absence?
current-affairs.fact: Based around Lake Naivasha, the 2021 event was won by France's Sébastien Ogier.

current-affairs.q: What is the Nairobi Expressway, opened in 2022?
current-affairs.fact: The roughly 27 km road links Jomo Kenyatta International Airport with Westlands, cutting journeys through city traffic.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, sprinter Ferdinand Omanyala won Commonwealth Games gold in which event?
current-affairs.fact: Kenya is famed for distance runners, making Omanyala's sprint gold in Birmingham especially celebrated at home.

current-affairs.q: At Paris 2024, Beatrice Chebet won the 5,000 m and which other Olympic title?
current-affairs.fact: She became the first Kenyan woman to win the Olympic 10,000 m title.

current-affairs.q: Who won the men's 800 m at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: He won in 1:41.19, holding off Canada's Marco Arop by just one hundredth of a second.

current-affairs.q: In May 2024, Beatrice Chebet became the first woman to run 10,000 m in under how many minutes?
current-affairs.fact: She clocked 28:54.14 at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene, Oregon.

current-affairs.q: Besides the 1,500 m and 5,000 m, in which event did Faith Kipyegon set a world record in summer 2023?
current-affairs.fact: She ran 4:07.64 in Monaco, completing a remarkable run of three world records in about seven weeks.

current-affairs.q: In September 2023, Eliud Kipchoge won the Berlin Marathon for a record how many times?
current-affairs.fact: Berlin was also where he set marathon world records in 2018 and 2022.

current-affairs.q: Kenya's 2019 national census counted roughly how many people?
current-affairs.fact: The census was the first in Kenya to be carried out using digital tablets for data collection.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, Kenya's government set a goal of growing how many trees by 2032?
current-affairs.fact: The campaign aims to restore about 10 million hectares of degraded land and raise tree cover to 30 per cent.

current-affairs.q: Which Kenyan won the men's 800 m at the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Compatriot Ferguson Rotich took silver, giving Kenya a one-two finish.

general.q: What is the capital of Kenya?
general.fact: Nicknamed the 'Green City in the Sun', Nairobi sits at about 1,800 metres above sea level.

general.q: Which Kenyan reserve hosts the Great Migration of wildebeest each year?
general.fact: Vast herds of wildebeest and zebras cross the crocodile-filled Mara River from Tanzania's Serengeti, usually from July to October.

general.q: What is the highest mountain in Kenya?
general.fact: At 5,199 metres, Mount Kenya is Africa's second-highest mountain, after Kilimanjaro in neighbouring Tanzania.

general.q: Kenya's Amboseli National Park is famous for views of elephants beneath which mountain, just across the border in Tanzania?
general.fact: Amboseli is renowned for its large, closely studied elephant herds, including famous big-tusked bulls.

general.q: Which line of latitude runs through Kenya, with roadside signs marking it near Nanyuki?
general.fact: Guides at the line sometimes demonstrate water swirling different ways on either side, a popular but unscientific trick.

general.q: Besides English, which is Kenya's other official language?
general.fact: Kiswahili is also Kenya's national language and a lingua franca across much of East Africa.

general.q: Ugali, Kenya's staple food, is a stiff porridge usually made from what?
general.fact: Ugali is eaten with the fingers, rolled into a ball and used to scoop up stews and greens.

general.q: Kenya shares Africa's largest lake with Uganda and Tanzania. Which lake is it?
general.fact: It is the largest tropical lake in the world and the main reservoir feeding the White Nile.

general.q: What are Kenya's colourful, privately run minibus taxis called?
general.fact: Many matatus are decorated with bold graffiti-style art and play loud music to attract passengers.

general.q: What makes Nairobi National Park unusual among Africa's parks?
choices: It lies within a capital city
It is above the snow line
general.fact: Founded in 1946 as Kenya's first national park, it lets visitors see lions and rhinos with skyscrapers in the background.

general.q: Which Rift Valley lake is famous for its huge flocks of pink flamingos?
general.fact: Flamingos gather to feed on algae that thrive in the lake's warm, alkaline waters.

general.q: Lake Turkana, in northern Kenya, is the world's largest what?
general.fact: Its striking blue-green colour earned it the nickname 'the Jade Sea'.

general.q: In which event did Kenyan men win every Olympic title they contested from 1968 to 2016?
general.fact: Kenya boycotted the 1976 and 1980 Games, but otherwise won steeplechase gold at every Olympics from 1968 to 2016.

general.q: Kip Keino won which event at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, launching Kenya's running fame?
general.fact: Keino won the 3,000 m steeplechase as well four years later in Munich.

general.q: At the London 2012 Olympics, David Rudisha set a world record in which event?
general.fact: His 1:40.91 made him the first person to run the distance in under 1 minute 41 seconds.

general.q: Which high-altitude Rift Valley town is nicknamed the 'Home of Champions' for its many elite runners?
general.fact: At about 2,400 metres, Iten attracts distance runners from around the world to train in its thin air.

general.q: What is Kenya's longest river?
general.fact: The Tana flows from the central highlands to the Indian Ocean, feeding several hydroelectric dams along the way.

general.q: What is the nickname of Kenya's national football team?
general.fact: The name comes from the national motto 'Harambee', meaning 'let us all pull together'.

general.q: Which Kenyan city is the country's main port on Lake Victoria?
general.fact: Kisumu grew up as the western terminus of the Uganda Railway, opened in 1901.

general.q: Kakamega Forest in western Kenya is the country's last remnant of which type of forest?
general.fact: It once formed the eastern edge of a rainforest belt stretching across central Africa, and it hosts hundreds of bird species.

general.q: Why do elephants on Mount Elgon venture deep into Kitum Cave?
choices: To mine salt from the cave walls
To drink from an underground lake
general.fact: Using their tusks, elephants scrape mineral-rich rock from the cave walls, gradually enlarging it over generations.

general.q: Which Kenyan lake is known for hot springs and geysers along its shores?
general.fact: Boiling water and steam burst from the shoreline, while flocks of flamingos feed in the shallows.

general.q: What is the name of Mount Kenya's highest peak?
general.fact: Batian (5,199 m) and nearby Nelion are named after 19th-century Maasai spiritual leaders.

general.q: Sudan, the world's last male northern white rhino, died in 2018 at which Kenyan conservancy?
general.fact: Only two northern white rhinos, both female, remained after his death, so scientists turned to assisted reproduction to save the subspecies.

general.q: Sukuma wiki, a popular Kenyan dish of sautéed greens, has a name that means what in Swahili?
general.fact: The cheap, filling greens help families stretch their budget until the end of the week.
